points.title: Passé composé vs imparfait : le choix final
points.explanationEn:
This unit closes out A2 by bringing together the two past tenses you've built up separately: the passé composé (completed, bounded actions — what happened) and the imparfait (ongoing states, habits, and descriptions — what was going on). By now you know how to form both. The remaining challenge, and the one that actually separates confident intermediate French from shaky French, is choosing correctly between them when telling a real story — especially since many verbs can grammatically appear in either tense, with the choice changing the meaning rather than being fixed by the verb itself.

Think of the imparfait as the tense of the background and the passé composé as the tense of the foreground. When you tell a story, the imparfait paints the unchanging scenery — the weather, people's ages and appearances, ongoing emotional or physical states, habitual routines, what was already in progress — while the passé composé marks the specific events that move the story forward, one after another. Il faisait nuit, il pleuvait, et le chat dormait tranquillement sous l'arbre quand, soudain, un renard est apparu (It was nighttime, it was raining, and the cat was sleeping peacefully under the tree when, suddenly, a fox appeared). Notice all three imparfait verbs describe an unchanging scene with no clear start or end point within the story, while est apparu is a single, sudden, bounded event — the moment the story actually happens.

A useful diagnostic: ask whether the action has clear boundaries — a beginning and an end that matter to the story — or whether it's better described as a state or backdrop with fuzzy edges. 'I lived in Provence for ten years' can go either way depending on what the speaker wants to emphasize: j'ai vécu en Provence pendant dix ans presents the ten years as a completed, bounded chapter of life (perhaps followed by 'and then I moved to Paris'), while j'habitais en Provence quand j'étais jeune presents it as a background situation with no particular endpoint in focus. This is why the passé composé/imparfait choice is often about the storyteller's perspective, not a fixed fact about the event itself — the same real-world situation can be described either way depending on what role it plays in the narrative.

Some verbs also shift meaning noticeably depending on which past tense is used, because the two tenses highlight different aspects of the same verb. Savoir in the imparfait (je savais) means 'I knew' (an ongoing state of knowledge), but in the passé composé (j'ai su) it means 'I found out' (the moment knowledge began — a bounded event). Similarly, connaître: je connaissais (I knew, was acquainted with) vs. j'ai connu (I met, became acquainted with). Vouloir: je voulais (I wanted, ongoing desire) vs. j'ai voulu (I decided to / tried to, often implying a specific attempt). Pouvoir: je pouvais (I was able to, capability in general) vs. j'ai pu (I managed to, succeeded in a specific instance). These meaning shifts aren't random exceptions — they follow the same underlying logic as everything else in this unit: imparfait = ongoing state, passé composé = the bounded moment something happened or changed. When telling any story about the past — a hike, a trip to see wildlife, an encounter with an animal — expect to weave both tenses together constantly: imparfait sets every scene, passé composé drives every event.

examples.fr: Il faisait beau et les oiseaux chantaient quand nous sommes arrivés à la forêt.
examples.en: The weather was nice and the birds were singing when we arrived at the forest.
examples.note: imparfait for background, passé composé for the arriving event

examples.fr: Le chat dormait sous l'arbre quand un renard est apparu.
examples.en: The cat was sleeping under the tree when a fox appeared.

examples.fr: Nous avons vu un cerf pendant notre randonnée.
examples.en: We saw a deer during our hike.

examples.fr: Quand j'étais petit, j'avais peur des araignées.
examples.en: When I was little, I was afraid of spiders.

examples.fr: Un jour, j'ai vu un ours près du camping et j'ai eu très peur.
examples.en: One day, I saw a bear near the campsite and I got very scared.
examples.note: specific bounded moment of fear, not an ongoing state: avoir peur in passé composé

examples.fr: Je savais que les loups vivaient dans cette région.
examples.en: I knew that wolves lived in that region.
examples.note: savais = ongoing knowledge, not a discovery

examples.fr: J'ai su la vérité seulement après le voyage.
examples.en: I found out the truth only after the trip.
examples.note: ai su = the moment of finding out

examples.fr: Il pleuvait pendant toute la randonnée, mais nous avons quand même profité du paysage.
examples.en: It rained during the whole hike, but we still enjoyed the scenery anyway.
examples.note: imparfait for the ongoing rain, passé composé for the completed enjoyment

examples.fr: Elle voulait voir des dauphins, alors elle a réservé une excursion en bateau.
examples.en: She wanted to see dolphins, so she booked a boat excursion.
examples.note: voulait = ongoing desire; a réservé = the resulting bounded action

examples.fr: Nous habitions près d'une forêt et nous voyions souvent des cerfs le matin.
examples.en: We used to live near a forest and we often saw deer in the morning.
examples.note: both habitual: imparfait for a repeated, non-bounded routine

commonMistakes: Defaulting to passé composé for the entire story because it feels like 'the past tense', even for clearly ongoing states or habits that call for imparfait (e.g. narrating 'il a fait beau' throughout a whole scene-setting passage).
Using imparfait for a single, clearly bounded event just because it happened 'a while ago', e.g. saying 'je voyais un ours' for one specific sighting instead of 'j'ai vu un ours'.

Not adjusting the translation of verbs like savoir, connaître, vouloir, and pouvoir between their imparfait and passé composé meanings, and instead treating them as always meaning the same thing regardless of tense.
Mixing tenses inconsistently within a single background description, e.g. switching to passé composé mid-description of the weather or setting without a narrative reason to do so.

Treating the choice as a fixed property of the verb itself (thinking 'this verb is an imparfait verb') rather than recognizing that most verbs can appear in either tense depending on what the sentence needs to express.
whyItTrips: English collapses both French past tenses into forms that overlap heavily ('I saw', 'I was seeing', 'I used to see' don't map cleanly onto a two-way split), so English speakers don't have a built-in instinct for when a boundary matters to the story and when it doesn't.

The tense choice frequently reflects the speaker's narrative perspective rather than an objective fact about the world, which feels unfamiliar and subjective to learners used to grammar rules being fixed and rule-based rather than interpretive.

Verbs like savoir, connaître, vouloir, and pouvoir genuinely change meaning across the two tenses, so learners can't rely on a single dictionary translation and must instead learn a meaning-pair for each verb — a category of learning English grammar never requires.
